# A coarse map, and a gate: what viewpoint invariance in VLMs is made of

*Workshop draft. Numbers in prose are regenerated by `bash bench/build_paper.sh`
and live in `paper/tables.md`, `paper/observers.csv`, `paper/ladder.csv` and
`figures/fig*.pdf`. Do not type a number into this file by hand.*

---

## 1. The claim

A model that can tell you which of four scenes you are looking at, and cannot
still tell you once you have walked around it, does not have a cognitive map.
It has an appearance gate.

We separate the two with a Four Mountains–style task. Every trial gives a study
view of a scene and four candidate views; exactly one is the same place. The
viewpoint change Δ between study and test is 0°, 45°, 90°, 135° or 180°, and the
appearance of the scene is re-sampled between study and test regardless, so
Δ = 0 is not a pixel match — it is the *gate*: same place, same bearing,
different appearance draw. Accuracy at Δ = 0 measures whether the observer can
do the task at all. Accuracy at Δ ≥ 45° measures what survives the walk.

Then we vary a second axis independently: **how near the foils are.** Foils are
drawn from a percentile band of rotation-optimal layout distance, and the three
banks ask the *same 500 questions* — same study scene, same azimuths, same
answer slot — differing only in which three foils sit beside the target. So
difficulty is a distance in metres over identical trials.

**The result, in one sentence: frontier models do carry viewpoint-invariant
place information, but it is coarse — it survives a 180° walk only while the
alternatives are tens of metres apart, and collapses when they are metres
apart. Open models below 100B never had it.**

Six findings.

1. **The foil-distance effect is enormous, and only frontier models have it**
   (Table 4, paired within-items). Rotated accuracy from the hard bank (median
   nearest foil 6.8 m) to the mid bank (31.4 m): Gemini 3.8 Flash 39% → 85%
   (exact McNemar p = 1.5e-10), GPT-5.6 Luna 31% → 55% (p = 0.002).
   Qwen2.5-VL-3B goes 29% → 25% (p = 0.65) and 7B 31% → 25% (p = 0.36) — no
   effect, because they are at chance at both. Same trials, same prompt, same
   token ceiling; only the neighbours moved.

   This is what "coarse" means, and it is why the headline is not "no map". A
   model with no spatial representation at all cannot show a 46-point foil
   effect. A model with a human-grade one would not need 30 m of separation to
   use it.

2. **Scale buys the gate and nothing past it — at any foil difficulty**
   (Figure 2). Across Qwen2.5-VL at 3B, 7B, 32B and 72B — one family, one
   prompt, one benchmark, size the only variable — gate accuracy climbs
   30% → 55% → 75% → 75%, while rotated accuracy goes 29% → 31% → 18% → 20%,
   crossing *below* chance. A 24× increase in parameters bought 45 points on the
   gate and cost 9 points on the walk.

   The obvious objection is that the hard bank is simply too hard for anything
   to move, so we repeated the axis with the foils 4.5× further away. It does
   not rescue the series: on the mid bank the rotated line is flat at
   25% → 25% → 28% across 3B, 7B and 32B, still at chance. The comparison with
   finding 1 is the paper in two lines — the *same* change in foil separation
   that takes Gemini from 39% to 85% moves Qwen2.5-VL by three points at any
   size. The frontier models have a coarse map that easier neighbours let them
   use; the open series has nothing to make easier.

3. **The gate and the walk are dissociated across observers too.** GPT-5.6 Luna
   and Qwen3-VL-235B both pass the gate (100% and 90%) and both land near chance
   rotated on the hard bank (31% and 19%). Qwen2.5-VL-3B fails the gate (30%)
   and lands in the same place (29%).

4. **The viewpoint curve is not monotonic: it bottoms out at Δ = 135°, not at
   180°** (Table 3). Pooled over the nine models, 23/180 correct at 135° —
   12.8% against 25% chance, one-sided binomial p = 4e-5 — recovering to 27% at
   a half turn. Six of the nine models have their own worst cell at 135°; the
   other three bottom out at 90°; none at 180°, which is the largest viewpoint
   change and should be hardest if rotation merely degraded a representation.

   Below chance is a systematic wrong answer, not weakness, and the recovery at
   exactly 180° says what the systematic answer is: a half-turn view of a
   roughly bilateral layout can be matched as a mirror image of the study view.
   That is right at 180° and actively wrong at 135°. The human is 5/5 at 135°.

5. **The models agree with each other about which trials are solvable, and not
   with the human** (Figure 5). Cohen's κ on trial-level correctness — high κ
   means the pair succeeds and fails on the same trials:
   model–model pairs average **κ = 0.24** (36 pairs, up to 0.61 between
   Qwen2.5-VL-72B and InternVL3-38B); human–model pairs average **κ = 0.07**
   (9 pairs, none above 0.15). Permutation p = 0.006. Nine models from four
   organisations are not failing independently. Gemini 3.8 Flash is the partial
   exception, at mean κ = 0.06 against the other models — outside the block.

   Kappa is symmetric under relabelling, so that matrix answers "agree on what
   they get right" and "agree on what they get wrong" with the same numbers.
   Figure 6 asks it without kappa: sort the 80 rotated trials by how many of
   the nine models solved each, and compare that curve against one built by
   shuffling every model's own correct/incorrect vector across trials. The real
   curve runs outside the shuffled band at both ends — **11 trials defeat all
   nine models where 6 are expected** — and the spread of trial difficulty is
   2.0× what independence predicts (permutation p = 0.0002). Difficulty is a
   property of the trial, shared across models from four organisations. Of those
   11 trials the human answered 4 and got 3 right.

   Ordering Figure 5 by similarity rather than by accuracy makes the structure
   plain: eight models form one warm block, and the two observers outside it are
   the human and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

6. **When a model is wrong, the error carries no information about geometry**
   (Figure 4). Each error offers three wrong answers — the nearest, middle and
   farthest foil in layout distance — and a graded representation should lean on
   the nearest. Pooled over 581 model errors the split is 30 / 39 / 32 against
   33 / 33 / 33, and no individual model departs from a third by more than its
   interval. **This is a null result**, reported as one; the human's errors do
   lean nearest (4/5) but that rests on five errors.

   Turning this from a null into a mechanism needs the appearance control:
   rank the options by embedding distance to the study image rather than by
   layout distance, and ask whether model choices track *that*. Errors random
   with respect to geometry but ordered with respect to appearance would show
   the paper's claim directly instead of inferring it. See §5.

**Reasoning does not help.** Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B in `thinking` mode scores 30%
against the `instruct` variant's 33%, with identical 19% rotated accuracy — same
model, same trials, same prompt, with and without extended reasoning. This is
the control for "it just needs to think longer".

**Five of the nine models do not beat their own positional prior** on rotated
trials (Table 1, `prior` column). Only the human (82% vs 26%) and Gemini (39% vs 24%) clear it
convincingly on the hard bank.

Paired against the human's 40 trials, every model is worse by exact McNemar
(Gemini p = 0.0002, Luna p = 0.0015, Qwen3-VL-235B p = 1e-6, Qwen2.5-VL-7B
p = 1e-5), and the effect survives restricting to rotated trials alone.

---

## 2. What the benchmark is

**Scenes.** Procedurally generated landscapes rendered in Blender, four peaks
per scene, 100 scenes. Every scene is rendered from five azimuths and two
appearance samples.

**Five stimulus modes**, a ladder that removes appearance cues while holding
spatial layout fixed:

| | |
|---|---|
| `c0_shape_colour` | objects differ in both shape and colour |
| `c1_shape` | shape only, colour held constant |
| `c2_colour` | colour only, shape held constant |
| `c3_peaks_bare` | bare terrain peaks, no objects |
| `c4_valley` | valley floor viewpoint, peaks at the horizon |

All five draw from one shared inventory of object morphologies — this was
checked directly after an earlier claim to the contrary turned out to be a stale
label in the layout metadata rather than a real inventory difference. The modes
differ in what appearance information is *available*, not in what objects exist.

**The difficulty ladder is within-items.** The three banks ask the *same 500
questions* — same study scene, same azimuths, same appearance draws, same answer
slot — and differ only in which three foils sit beside the target
(`build_hard_benchmark.py --match`). This matters: built independently, the
bands each choose their own target scenes, and 483 of 500 study scenes differed
between the random and hard banks, so any cross-band comparison would have been
confounded by which places were asked about. Matched, an observer's accuracy
across banks is a psychometric curve in metres over identical trials
(Table 4).

**Foils are a controlled difficulty axis in metres.** For every pair of scenes
we compute a rotation-optimal, identity-matched layout distance

> D(i,j) = min over φ of mean over objects k of ‖R(φ)·p_ik − p_jk‖

— the residual after the best rigid rotation, so it measures layout difference
and not bearing. Foils are then drawn from a percentile band of that distance:

| bank | band | file |
|---|---|---|
| random | — | `data/vlm_benchmark_4afc.json` |
| easy | 90–100th pct | `data/vlm_benchmark_4afc_easy.json` |
| **hard (this paper's arm)** | **0–10th pct** | `data/vlm_benchmark_4afc_hard.json` |
| very hard | 0–2nd pct | `data/vlm_benchmark_4afc_vhard.json` |

Percentile bands are computed **per mode**, not in absolute metres. An earlier
absolute-metre cut produced a U-shaped difficulty curve that turned out to be a
mode confound: 32 of the 37 shortest-distance trials were c3 or c4.

**The human arm is the same task in a browser** (`human_task_hard/`), the same
trial ids, the same four images in a 2×2 grid, with autosave to `localStorage`
so a session can be resumed. The only difference from the model arm is the
prompt style: models get `cot_anyview`, people get `neutral_anyview`, which is
the same instruction without the "think step by step" scaffold.

---

## 3. Two bugs that invalidated earlier numbers

Both are worth a paragraph in the paper, because both are easy to reproduce and
neither is visible in a result file.

**The prompt asserted its own answer.** Six of nine prompt styles told the model
the test views were *"shown from a different viewpoint"* — on every trial,
including the Δ = 0 trials where it was false. Gemini 3.8 Flash went from 5/10
to 10/10 on Δ = 0 trials on a one-clause change (p = 0.031), which is why the
locked prompt says "It may be viewed from the same direction as the study image
or from a different one". Every number in this paper uses the fixed prompt, and
`run_config.prompt_sha256_12` in each result file hashes the literal instruction
text rather than the style name.

**A token ceiling read as a difficulty effect.** The random-foil arm ran at
`max_tokens=4000` and the hard-foil arm at 8000. Half the c4 replies in the
short arm were truncated mid-reasoning and scored wrong, which looked exactly
like "c4 is the hardest mode" until the two configs were diffed. `max_tokens` is
now part of the locked arm and is stamped into every result file.

**A note on the 32B and 72B numbers.** That larger models score *below* their
own answer prior on rotated trials is surprising enough that we audited it
before believing it. No reply was truncated (longest 2 704 characters against an
8 000-token ceiling); no reply failed to parse; all 100 replies from each model
matched the strongest extraction pattern, an explicit "Final Answer: Option N",
and hand-checked samples parse faithfully — including cases where the model's
own prose identifies one option as matching and then names another. The
appearance gate is intact at 75% for both, which a broken pipeline would have
depressed. And Qwen2.5-VL-32B *improves* on the mid foil bank, 14/80 → 22/80
rotated, so the model and the pipeline both work; it is the near foils that
defeat it. The effect survives correcting for each model's own answer prior
(Table 1, *vs prior*).

**A defect the audit did surface.** The answer key of the 100-trial slice is
16/29/29/26, and 11/22/26/21 on the rotated trials, although the 500-trial bank
it was drawn from is exactly 125 each. The stratified subsample balances mode
and viewpoint change and takes no care of the answer slot. An observer that
happens to avoid answering "1" is rewarded by a few points for no reason
connected to the task — Qwen2.5-VL-7B answers "4" on 55% of rotated trials. The
fix that costs nothing is the *vs prior* column, which is what the text quotes;
the fix that costs a re-run is a slice balanced on the answer slot as well, and
it should be done before the camera-ready.

---

## 4. Reproducing every number

```bash
bash bench/build_paper.sh
```

`bench/collate.py` is the only script that opens a result file. It validates
every run against `bench/paper_spec.py` — one benchmark, one prompt hash, one
token ceiling, one 100-trial slice — and separates **blocking deviations** (the
run measured something else; excluded from the headline table) from
**provenance gaps** (the run predates config stamping; reported, not dropped).
It then writes `paper/{runs,observers,cells,trials}.csv`, and the table and
figure scripts read only those. A figure and a table therefore cannot disagree
about an accuracy.

---

## 5. What is still open

- **The human arm is 40/100.** Every human number here is a partial run and is
  marked as such in every table and figure.
- **One participant.** A second and third are needed before the human column is
  a baseline rather than an existence proof.
- **No human on the foil ladder.** Table 4 has no human row, so "models need
  tens of metres of foil separation and people do not" is argued from the model
  side alone. Forty human trials on the mid bank would close it.
- **A slice balanced on the answer slot**, so raw accuracy needs no prior
  correction.
- **Prompt sweep**: Qwen2.5-VL-32B across six prompt styles on the locked
  benchmark, running. Read on rotated trials only — six of the nine styles
  assert a rotation that is false at Δ=0 and true everywhere else.
- **The ladder is filling in.** Table 4 has the frontier models at all three
  rungs and the open models part-way; the remaining runs are queued on dgx2.
- **A second family for the scaling axis.** Qwen2.5-VL runs 3B → 72B; InternVL3
  contributes a single 38B point. One family is an existence proof, not a
  scaling law.
- **7/100 of Qwen3-VL-235B-instruct's replies did not parse** and are scored
  wrong. That is the honest default but it flatters nobody; worth a re-parse.
